title: He guides the heart
hook: no calamity strikes except by Allah's leave, and whoever believes, He guides his heart (64:11)
carry: he guides the heart through it

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't let them distract you, and your line was remember through it all. Did you find one breath in the busiest moment? Today, Surah At-Taghabun. Day six hundred thirty, the end of the week.

Medina, a small house. A woman named Umm Salama has just lost her husband, Abu Salama, and the grief is still new. She remembers something the Prophet ﷺ had taught: words to say when a loss strikes. She starts to say them, and then stops, thinking: who could be better than Abu Salama? She says them anyway. Hold that moment. Today's verse is about what happens inside a heart at exactly that point.

Surah At-Taghabun, verse eleven. Pickthall: "No calamity befalleth save by Allah's leave. And whosoever believeth in Allah, He guideth his heart." The word for calamity is musiba, anything that strikes, from a root meaning to hit the mark. The verse makes two claims. First, nothing happens outside God's permission. Second, and this is the tender part: for the one who believes, God guides the heart. Not removes the calamity. Guides the heart through it. A student of the companions named 'Alqama explained the verse simply. It's the person struck by a loss, he said, who knows it is from God, and so accepts it and is content. Guidance here isn't an answer to why. It's a steadiness that comes in the middle of the not-knowing. Back to Umm Salama. Muslim records the words the Prophet had taught: we belong to God and to him we return; O God, reward me in my calamity and give me something better in its place. The first half is from the Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah. Pickthall: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Umm Salama said it, doubting. Later, the Prophet himself asked to marry her, and she became one of the mothers of the believers. She'd say afterward that God had given her better than Abu Salama: the Messenger of God. The verse doesn't promise the story always turns out like hers. It promises something smaller and closer: a guided heart, steadied in the loss, before anything else changes.
screen: `MUSIBA: WHAT STRIKES.` · `NOT REMOVED, BUT GUIDED THROUGH.` · `WE ARE GOD'S, AND TO HIM WE RETURN.` · `UMM SALAMA SAID IT, DOUBTING.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept one setback calmly. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one recent setback, not the biggest grief, something smaller: a plan that fell through, a no, a loss of time or money. Let yourself feel it honestly. Then, if you pray, say the words Umm Salama said: we belong to God, and to him we return. If not, simply breathe out slowly and let your shoulders drop, accepting that it happened. The bell holds the time.
He guides the heart. No calamity strikes except by God's leave, and whoever believes in God, he guides that person's heart. Today's word.

Your line: he guides the heart through it. This week ran from say it, do it, through God's helpers and the Friday prayer, to propped-up timber, distraction and Umm Salama's words. Today, meet one setback calmly. Day six hundred thirty.

howItsDone: When news of a loss comes, Muslims widely say 'inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un', we belong to God and to him we return, and many add the supplication the Prophet taught Umm Salama.

fork.setup: you're Umm Salama. your husband has died, and you remember the words to say. you think: who could be better than him? what do you do?
options: stay silent; the words feel untrue.
wait until the grief has passed.
fork.reveal: she said them anyway, and later married the Prophet. she said God had given her better than Abu Salama.

original.note: Arabic: he guides his heart. qalb is the heart; the verb is from h-d-y, guidance.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything that happens is God's will, so don't complain.
what it means: nothing strikes outside God's leave, and the believer's heart is guided through what strikes.
what a scholar hears: musiba in 64:11; 'Alqama's gloss reported in Bukhari's tafsir; Umm Salama's supplication in Muslim 918; 2:156 as the istirja'.
